quiz.q: What does `#[tokio::main]` do to `async fn main`?
options: Nothing at runtime — it's just documentation
Rewrites `main` into an ordinary function that builds a Tokio runtime and blocks on your async body
Spawns `main`'s body on a background thread and returns immediately
Converts `main` into a `macro_rules!` macro
quiz.explain: The macro expands to a plain fn main that builds a Tokio runtime (e.g. Builder::new_multi_thread().build()) and calls .block_on(...) with your async body — that block_on is the executor driving your futures.

options: The future's result directly, synchronously
A `JoinHandle` you can `.await` later to get the task's result
Nothing — spawned tasks are always fire-and-forget
A brand new Tokio runtime
quiz.explain: tokio::spawn schedules the future to run concurrently and immediately hands back a JoinHandle. Awaiting the handle waits for the task and yields its return value.

quiz.q: Why must a task passed to `tokio::spawn` be `'static` and `Send`?
options: It's an arbitrary limitation with no real reason
The task can be moved between worker threads and may outlive the function that spawned it, so it can't safely borrow local data or hold non-thread-safe types
Because Tokio can only ever run on a single OS thread
Because async functions are never allowed to capture variables
quiz.explain: Tokio's scheduler can migrate a task across worker threads at any .await point, and the task may run long after its spawning function returns — so it must fully own everything it touches, and that data must be thread-safe.

quiz.q: `tokio::spawn(async { println!("{name}"); })` fails to compile with error E0373 because it borrows `name` from the enclosing function. What's the fix?
options: Change `async` to `async move` so the task owns its own copy of `name`
Change `name`'s type from `String` to `&str`
Remove the `println!` call entirely
Wrap the whole block in `unsafe { }`
quiz.explain: async move captures name by value instead of by reference, so the spawned task no longer depends on the spawning function's stack frame — satisfying the 'static requirement.

options: Runs `a`, then runs `b` after `a` finishes
Runs `a` and `b` concurrently and returns once BOTH have finished
Runs whichever of `a` or `b` finishes first and drops the other
Spawns `a` and `b` onto independent OS threads with no coordination between them
quiz.explain: join! drives all its futures concurrently on the same task and only completes once every one of them is done, returning a tuple of their results.

quiz.q: In `tokio::select! { a => ..., b => ... }`, what happens to the branch that does NOT finish first?
options: It keeps running in the background until it eventually finishes
It is dropped/cancelled immediately once the other branch wins
It causes a compile error
It automatically retries from the start
quiz.explain: select! polls all branches concurrently; the instant one completes, its arm runs and every other branch is dropped mid-flight — it is not resumed or finished later.

quiz.q: Why does calling `std::thread::sleep` inside an async task cause a real performance problem, even though the code compiles fine?
options: It doesn't actually cause any problem
It freezes the entire OS worker thread it's running on, so every other task scheduled on that same thread is stalled until it returns
It only slows down the task that called it and nothing else
It silently crashes the whole program
quiz.explain: std::thread::sleep never yields — it blocks the worker thread outright. On a runtime with limited worker threads, that stalls every other task sharing that thread, not just the caller.

quiz.q: What's the right tool for running real blocking or CPU-heavy work inside an async program without stalling other tasks?
options: `tokio::join!`
`tokio::select!`
`tokio::task::spawn_blocking`
Just calling it directly inside the `async fn`
quiz.explain: spawn_blocking moves the closure onto a separate thread pool dedicated to blocking work, so it never occupies (and stalls) the async worker threads.

quiz.q: Which of these is a telltale sign that async code has no runtime actually driving it?
options: The program compiles and runs exactly as expected
A compile error about needing async context, or a runtime panic like 'there is no reactor running'
The program runs noticeably faster than a synchronous version
Nothing different happens at all — it's indistinguishable
quiz.explain: Missing #[tokio::main]/the tokio dependency shows up either as a compile-time error (.await needs async context) or, if you tried to drive a future manually without a reactor, a runtime panic complaining no runtime/reactor is running.

flashcards.back: Rewrites `async fn main` into an ordinary `fn main` that builds a Tokio runtime (roughly `Builder::new_multi_thread().enable_all().build()`) and blocks on your async body with `.block_on(...)`.

flashcards.front: What does `tokio::spawn` do, and what does it return?
flashcards.back: Schedules a future to run concurrently on Tokio's worker pool. Returns a `JoinHandle` you can `.await` to get the task's result.

flashcards.front: What two bounds must a spawned future satisfy, and why?
flashcards.back: `'static` (owns everything it touches) and `Send` (safe to move across threads) — because the task can migrate between worker threads and may outlive the function that spawned it.

flashcards.front: How do you fix `tokio::spawn(async { ... })` erroring E0373 because it borrows a local?
flashcards.back: Add `move`: `tokio::spawn(async move { ... })`, so the task owns a copy of the data instead of borrowing it.
`join!` runs all its futures concurrently and waits for ALL of them to finish. `select!` races them and proceeds with whichever finishes FIRST, cancelling the rest.

flashcards.front: Why does `std::thread::sleep` inside an async task hurt performance?
flashcards.back: It blocks the entire OS worker thread it runs on — every other task scheduled on that thread stalls until the sleep call returns. Use `tokio::time::sleep` instead.

flashcards.front: What should you use for real blocking or CPU-heavy work inside an async program?
flashcards.back: `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` — it moves the work onto a separate thread pool so it doesn't stall the async worker threads.

flashcards.front: What error appears when `tokio::spawn`'s future borrows a non-`'static` local?
flashcards.back: E0373: "async block may outlive the current function, but it borrows `x`, which is owned by the current function." Fix with `async move`.
